title: Daughters and sons
hook: He gives daughters to whom He wills, sons, or both, or none (42:49–50)

segments.voice: Yesterday, their affairs by consultation, and your line was consult. Did you ask someone before deciding something that touched them? Day five hundred sixty-nine.

In seventh-century Arabia, the Qur'an describes a scene it clearly wants to end. A man is told his wife has given birth to a girl. His face darkens. He hides from people, ashamed of the news, wondering whether to keep her or bury her in the dust. Surah An-Nahl paints it; Surah At-Takwir says the buried girl will one day be asked for what sin she was killed. Against that background, listen to the order of the words in Surah Ash-Shura, when it talks about children. Who gets named first.

Verse forty-nine. To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Pickthall: "He createth what He will." Then: He gives daughters to whomever He wills, and sons to whomever He wills. Daughters first. In a culture where a daughter's birth could darken a father's face, the Qur'an lists girls ahead of boys, as gifts. Some early scholars noticed this; one is reported to have said that it's a blessing for a woman when her first child is a girl, because Allah began with daughters. Verse fifty continues: or He gives both, sons and daughters, and He makes whom He wills childless. He is Knowing, Able. Four possibilities: daughters, sons, both, or none. Every one of them is placed in Allah's hands. Which means none of them is a verdict on the parents. Not a reward for having sons. Not a punishment for having daughters, or no children at all. The Qur'an's own stories show it. Ibrahim and Zakariyya waited into old age. 'A'isha, the Prophet's wife, had no children, and she became one of the most important teachers in early Islam. The Prophet ﷺ himself had sons who died young, and it was through his daughter Fatima that his family continued. And a hadith in Sahih Muslim gives raising girls a special honor: whoever raises two daughters until they're grown, the Prophet said, will come on the Day of Resurrection with me like this, and he held two fingers together. The verse lists four gifts, and the hadith makes sure the first one is never treated as the lesser.

The practice: thank Allah for the children around you. Sit, and bring them to mind one by one: your own, if you have them, or nieces and nephews, neighbors' kids, students, a friend's baby, the child you once were. Picture each face for a breath. If you pray, thank Allah for each one. If not, simply be grateful. And if there's an ache here, a child hoped for or lost, let it be part of the sitting too. The bell holds the time.
Daughters and sons. Ash-Shura forty-nine and fifty: Allah gives daughters, sons, both, or none, and daughters are named first. Today's word.
Your line: each gift is his. Today, say something kind to or about a girl in your life, a daughter, a niece, a student, and let her hear that she's a gift. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims greet the birth of a child with thanks to Allah and often an 'aqiqah celebration for both girls and boys; the hadith on raising daughters is widely taught as an honor for parents of girls.

fork.setup: in a culture where some men grieved at a daughter's birth, the Qur'an lists the gifts of children. which does it name first?
fork.reveal: daughters, then sons, then both, then none: every one of them Allah's to give.

original.note: Arabic: He gives daughters to whom He wills; yahab is the verb of giving a gift (hiba).

trapdoor: what you thought: God decides whether you have kids.
what it means: daughters, sons, both or none are each Allah's gift, and daughters are named first.

what a scholar hears: yahab (from hiba, a free gift) governs inathan before dhukur in 42:49; tafsir records the remark about a firstborn daughter; Muslim 2631 honors raising daughters, against the background of 16:58–59 and 81:8–9.

sources.ref: tafsir on 42:49 (a firstborn daughter as a blessing, attributed to Wathila ibn al-Asqa')
